title: Michael Caputo Consults for Ukraine’s Bloc Lytvyn in 2007
description_short: Michael Caputo moved to Ukraine in 2007 to work as a political consultant for Bloc Lytvyn.
description_medium: In 2007, political consultant Michael Caputo left Miami Beach for Ukraine to work for Bloc Lytvyn, the party led by Volodymyr Lytvyn. The supplied timeline notes Lytvyn’s Russian award and photograph with Vladimir Putin, as well as Caputo’s earlier work for Gazprom Media. It does not establish Kremlin direction, a political takeover, or a Trump connection to this episode.
description_long: In 2007, political consultant Michael Caputo left Miami Beach for Ukraine to work for Bloc Lytvyn, the party led by Volodymyr Lytvyn. The supplied timeline links Lytvyn to Russia by noting that he received the Russian Order of Friendship and was photographed with Vladimir Putin. It also notes Caputo’s earlier work for Gazprom Media in Russia. These facts describe Caputo’s professional history and the political setting around the party, but they do not establish that Putin hired or directed him. The supplied account provides no contract, communications or other evidence connecting the Ukrainian campaign to a Russian political operation. Nor does it show that the campaign represented a “political takeover.” Caputo’s later association with Donald Trump does not itself turn this earlier consulting work into an action by Trump. The event can be described as Caputo’s move to Ukraine for campaign consulting, while claims about Kremlin direction and a takeover require evidence beyond nationality, prior employment and a photograph.

title: Donald Trump and Dmitry Rybolovlev cross paths twice in a week
description_medium: A 2016 campaign timeline says Donald Trump’s campaign aircraft and a plane associated with Dmitry Rybolovlev were at airports in Las Vegas and Charlotte around October 30 and November 3. It describes possible aircraft overlaps, not a confirmed meeting. The timeline did not load during the focused source check, so its underlying flight records could not be assessed.
description_long: A timeline published after the 2016 campaign reports two occasions when Donald Trump’s campaign aircraft and a plane associated with Dmitry Rybolovlev were at the same airports. title: Justice Department’s Housing Discrimination Case Against Trump Management
description_short: A 1973 Justice Department suit alleged that Trump Management discriminated against Black housing applicants; a 1975 consent decree resolved the case without an admission of liability.
description_medium: In 1973, the Justice Department sued Fred and Donald Trump and Trump Management, alleging Fair Housing Act violations across 39 buildings with more than 14,000 apartments. The complaint said white testers were told of vacancies while Black testers were not or were steered elsewhere; it also alleged employees coded Black applicants. A 1975 consent decree barred discrimination but expressly included no admission of liability.
description_long: In October 1973, the Justice Department filed a Fair Housing Act case against Fred Trump, Donald Trump and Trump Management. The complaint alleged discriminatory rental practices at 39 buildings containing more than 14,000 apartments. It cited testing in which white prospective tenants were told of vacancies while Black testers were not or were steered to other buildings, and alleged that employees used codes to identify Black applicants. The defendants counterclaimed against the government; the court dismissed that claim and allowed the housing case to proceed. The parties resolved the case through a consent decree signed in June 1975. It prohibited discrimination and specified practices including misrepresenting apartment availability, required fair-housing advertisements, and arranged for the New York Urban League to receive vacancy lists and refer applicants for some openings. The decree expressly said the settlement was not an admission of a violation. The complaint’s allegations and the decree’s requirements are documented, but the settlement should not be described as a court finding that the defendants admitted liability.

notes: The Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case summary was read directly. The unsupported doorman instructions, specific “C”/“No. 9” codes, and asserted downstream effects have been removed; allegations are distinguished from findings.
